legal cornice ceiling 17.55 m for a 12.00 m street; built to 12.99 m (74% of it) — the law says how tall you may build, programme and money say how tall you did.
  · era second_empire (Règlement du 27 juillet 1859)
  · street width 12.00 m -> legal cornice ceiling 17.55 m (Règlement du 27 juillet 1859)
  · roof envelope diagonal_45: ridge 3.20 m above the cornice (legal max 3.20 m)
  · garret storeys: a second storey of chambres de bonne costs 2.90 m of the 17.55 m legal cornice, which would leave 14.65 m of stone under it — less than the 14.81 m a trade floor, its entresol and three letting storeys need. The servants in the roof are the servants of the households below, and there would not be enough of them
  · class modest: facade ambition 0.74 (INFERRED, only the ordering is contractual) -> facade target 12.99 m (74% of the 17.55 m the stone face may fill)
  · entrance: the entrance is a porte piétonne (2.35 m of frontage, ABSOLUTE): a modest household does not keep a carriage, and a porte cochère costs a frontage bay, a passage and a cour behind it
  · ground floor (shop): 3.95 m (SOURCED — Daly 1864 (Sér. 1 Vol. 1 t. 2), rez-de-chaussée floor-to-floor over 16 buildings: median 3.95 m, range 3.42-4.85 m, class medians 4.20 / 3.95 / 3.81 m. The ladder falls 9 % across the whole social range while the ranges overlap almost completely, so the commercial ground storey is ABSOLUTE and class-independent (scale-bar measured, ±10 %, with the 125 Champs-Élysées printed ladder anchoring the Première end))
  · storey minimum 2.60 m (Règlement du 27 juillet 1859)
  · typical storey band [2.60, 3.07, 3.41] m: a plain storey of 2.60 m (a room a person lives in, plus the floor structure carrying the one above) plus the margin ambition buys above it — class modest scales the MARGIN only, never the plain storey inside it
  · entresol: ground floor (shop) wants an entresol, but class modest only gives up the height where 4 letting storey(s) still stand over it: that needs 19.28 m and the facade budget is 12.99 m
  · facade target 12.99 m rounded to 12.99 m — the height a whole-storey stack can actually fill over 3.95 m of fixed slot(s), capped by the 17.55 m legal ceiling. The fraction is a target, not a quota, and a section is built of whole storeys
  · [vertical] budget 12.9870 m
  · [vertical] 1 fixed slot(s) reserve 3.9500 m at exactly their preferred width — absolute, so they never absorb
  · [vertical] 2 bay(s) at preferred 3.0675 m, centreline to centreline = 6.1350 m
  · [vertical] added 1 module(s), stepping by 1: 2 -> 3 bays
  · [vertical] slack -0.1655 m
  · [vertical] narrowed the filler in each bay by 0.0552 m (0.1655 m absorbed)
  · [vertical] rung ADD_MODULE; residual 0.000e+00 m
  · taper: 3 typical storey(s) at rate 0.93 (INFERRED), held inside [2.60, 3.41] m -> [3.233, 3.007, 2.797] m, bottom to top
  · comble CEILING 7.00 m over the 12.99 m eaves it springs from — the égout du toit, where the decree springs it, not the legal cornice: the gabarit's top is 20.75 m above the pavement (17.55 m legal cornice + 3.20 m comble), and the 4.56 m of cornice height this facade declined to build is legal height the roof still has over it — not height the roof forfeited with it. The same curve is simply traced to a taller top, which costs 7.00 m of inset against the 3.20 m a comble sprung from the cornice would need, and the parcel is what says whether that is affordable
  · comble BUILT 3.20 m — sized by the garret storeys it holds, inside the decree's own 3.20 m allowance sprung from these eaves, and not up to the 7.00 m ceiling over them. A8.5: building to the ceiling made the roof grow by exactly what the facade declined, so the sum never moved and every building in the city reached its legal total. Nothing here reads the class — a comble is floor, not show — so the 3.80 m left under the ceiling is legal volume nobody had a use for
  · the plot: a 14.00 m parcel stands 2 whole band(s) of brisis with a room behind them — a room needs 2.00 m of floor between the two opposing slopes under 2.20 m of standing height, and on a shallow plot the slopes meet before the next band has it. This is what the cornice may not read (A15.1): the cornice runs across the party wall and parcel depths do not, so the plot limits what gets BUILT and never what was given up for it
  · comble section: a brisis of 2.90 m — 1 × 2.90 m ((a room a person lives in, plus the floor structure carrying the one above) + (the wall plate the terrasson's rafters land on, over the garret's ceiling)) — standing on the gabarit, then a terrasson at 12° closing the remaining 0.30 m over the 4.10 m back to the middle of the plot. The fold is what makes it a comble BRISÉ (A8.3)
  · comble holds a storey (1 of 1): 2.60 m clear, its floor at 12.99 m, behind band 1 of a 2.90 m brisis, inside a 3.20 m roof, with 8.80 m of floor between the slopes at its ceiling (a room needs 2.00 m — a garret room needs a bed's length of floor under full height)
  · bay pitch 2.80 m, held in [2.70, 3.40] m — the narrowest REPEATING bay a window and its two piers make sense in / the widest bay a stone lintel and the joist run behind it will span. The rhythm is what the masonry spans, so it is very nearly the same on every frontage in Paris; a modest builder moves it by 0.25 m and buys the rest of what the money shows in the OPENING inside the bay, in storey height and in ornament (A8.6)
  · porte_pietonne: 2.35 m of frontage — the clear opening plus the jamb its head lands on either side (((SOURCED — Daly 1864 (César Daly, L'Architecture privée au XIXme siècle sous Napoléon III, Sér. 1 Vol. 1 t. 2), median of eight portes piétonnes measured in Deuxième Classe (1.61-1.91 m); the printed callouts '1.760' at 87 boulevard de Sébastopol and '1.630' at 9 rue du Conservatoire bracket it (printed dimension on the plate)) + (INFERRED — the jamb carrying the head over a pedestrian entrance; a shorter span than a carriage arch, so a thinner pier, and neither figure knows what the building cost)) + (INFERRED — the jamb carrying the head over a pedestrian entrance; a shorter span than a carriage arch, so a thinner pier, and neither figure knows what the building cost)). entrance placed ON the axis: 1 bay(s) either side of it in a run of 2 — a positional rule, not a remainder
  · which is 1.05 m less frontage than a porte_cochere would have taken — on a narrow parcel a difference that size is a whole window axis, carried up every storey. Which door a frontage has is entitlement and not ambition, so this is the one thing on the facade that buys windows or spends them (A10.2)

this storey stands inside the comble — its floor at 12.987 m is the top of the stone face, not a level behind it — so nothing on the stone facade is composed on it: no opening, no surround, no keystone, no balcon filant, no cornice. What encloses it is the roof, and its windows are the lucarnes the termination phase stands on that roof, one per bay of this very storey's grid. Emitted empty rather than omitted, because it is still a floor of the building and still has the role the stack gave it.

comble inscribed in the diagonal_45 envelope: 3.200 m tall over eaves at 12.987 m — the top of the legal solid (20.750 m) reckoned from those eaves, capped by the parcel where its two slopes meet — ridge set back 7.000 m, approximated as a broken mansard of 45.0° / 12.0° breaking at 68% of its height. Nobody chose the angle — it is the boundary of the legal solid for a 12.00 m street.

dormer-and-ornament repertoire drawn from the variants genuinely in use at 1865 for a modest building: small_plain_dormers 100%. The comble under them is a diagonal_45 because the decree says so, which is a different kind of fact and is not on this axis

trace.detail: the comble is a diagonal_45 because the decree in force says so, and for no other reason: geometry is a step on the decree date and carries no class lag, while 'small_plain_dormers' is fashion and does. The two are free to be out of step — a lagged builder fitting pedimented lucarnes to an arc comble is the straggler the brief calls the common case — and neither may be inferred from the other, so no variant on the fashion axis is allowed to name a comble geometry.

covering 'zinc_roofing': zinc stood at 39% prevalence at 1865 for a modest building, and the material axis is drawn separately from the dormer axis because a zinc roof and a pedimented dormer are not alternatives

trace.detail: section through the building on a plane perpendicular to the street: pavement to eaves at 12.987 m up the facade plane, then the brisis ON the diagonal_45 envelope to the fold 2.174 m above the eaves, then the terrasson to a ridge 3.200 m above them and 7.000 m back from the facade — 4 point(s). The brisis is not chosen: it is the boundary of the legal solid, sampled, because a builder takes every centimetre of garret floor the law allows. What stands above it IS chosen — it is a roof, not an envelope (A8.3) — and it is inscribed inside the same boundary.

the fold is at 2.174 m over the eaves, 67.9% of the comble, and 2.174 m back from the facade — where the terrasson, arriving at the ridge 7.000 m back, meets the diagonal_45 envelope on its way down (A12.1). It is NOT the 2.900 m the garret's own wall stands: that number is a count of whole chambres de bonne and it puts the fold within 0.300 m of the ridge, leaving a hairline terrasson and a flat deck across the rest of the plot — a slab with a nick near the top rather than a comble brisé. The section is over-determined once the terrasson's pitch is fixed, so the SAME three numbers are read as a terrasson running the whole way to the ridge and a fold wherever that line crosses the gabarit. The ridge did not move (3.200 m, the decree's and the measured plates'); only the fold did, and it slid down the envelope, so it is still a point setback_at returned.

the comble springs from the eaves the building actually has (12.987 m, the sum of its storeys), not from the legal cornice ceiling (17.55 m) — the diagonal springs from the égout du toit, so a building that stopped short of its ceiling carries the whole roof SHAPE down with it. Its CEILING does not come down with it: 4.563 m of cornice height went unbuilt, and that is legal space the building declined to occupy rather than space it forfeited, so the SAME curve is traced to a taller top and the comble MAY stand 7.000 m over these eaves — 3.800 m more than the 3.200 m the ridge stands over the cornice — on a parcel with 7.000 m to give. The springing did not move; only the top did (A3.1). It does NOT stand there: a ceiling is not a height, and building to it made the roof grow by exactly what the stone gave up, so every immeuble in Paris came out at its legal total (A8.5). What was built is 3.200 m — the garret storeys behind the brisis and the terrasson closing over them — set back 7.000 m, leaving 3.800 m of legal volume nobody had a use for. This silhouette is inscribed below the envelope sprung from its own eaves (worst margin +0.000 m); measured from the legal cornice — the weaker line, which is not the test — it would be +0.000 m. A margin of exactly zero is the facade standing on the street line, which is where a Paris facade stands.
ends 'party_wall': a corner building's comble is hipped and shows this profile at its returns; a mid-block one runs straight between party walls. Decided here so the renderer decides nothing.
